voice_note: FACT lines are neutral and past-tense. CONTEXT adds short history and threads stories together. CONSTITUTIONAL register argues founding-intent by framing, grounded in primary founding sources, never preaching, never settled. PREDICTIVE register is falsifiable. Sources shown outlet-name-only. national.headline: U.S. strikes Iran for a fifth day; Hormuz blockade back on
national.fact: U.S. Central Command struck targets across Iran for a fifth straight day on July 15, hitting command centers, air-defense sites, and an army barracks. At least seven Iranian troops were killed and about 260 people wounded, CNN reported. The U.S. reimposed its naval blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran fired missiles and drones at U.S. allies in the Gulf and warned of a wider war.
national.context: The ceasefire held eight days. President Trump declared it over on July 8, after Iran's Revolutionary Guard struck three commercial ships — one a Qatari gas tanker — off Oman. The fighting since has not stayed between Iran and Israel. Iran's missiles have come down on Qatar, and its blockade closes the channel that carries a fifth of the world's oil past the coasts of Saudi Arabia, the Emirates, Kuwait, and Iraq. Every Gulf state is now a party to a war Tehran calls a fight with Israel.
national.predictive: The strait is the pressure point. Transits are already down more than half. If they stay near zero past July 17, when the U.S. oil waiver lapses, Brent moves through $90 and the war's cost lands on every economy that buys oil — not only the combatants. The broken ceasefire is now the least likely of the three roads out; escalation and a forced reopening are the other two.

national.headline: Israel and Lebanon agree how the first withdrawals happen — not when
national.fact: Israeli and Lebanese delegations ended two days of U.S.-brokered talks in Rome on July 15 with an agreement on how Israel will pull its forces from two pilot zones in southern Lebanon. The Lebanese army will move in to keep the areas clear of Hezbollah weapons. No date was set for the withdrawals.
national.context: It was the sixth round, and the first since a framework signed in Washington in June. The structure is agreed; the hard part is not. Hezbollah has rejected both the deal and any move to disarm it — and it holds the ground the Lebanese army is meant to fill.
national.predictive: A deal with no timeline and an armed party that rejects it is a test of enforcement, not diplomacy. Watch whether the Lebanese army actually enters the first pilot zone. If it does and holds, the framework has teeth. If the date keeps slipping, this joins the long list of southern-Lebanon withdrawals announced and not made.

national.headline: House keeps $3.3B in Israel aid; the coalition to cut it crosses both parties
national.fact: The House rejected an amendment from Rep. Thomas Massie, 104 to 314, that would have cut $3.3 billion in military aid to Israel from the 2027 security spending bill. Massie, a Kentucky Republican, was the only Republican to vote for it. Democrats split almost evenly — 103 for, 98 against.
national.context: The vote cut across both parties in a way few do. Minority Whip Katherine Clark and Nancy Pelosi voted to strip the aid; Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries voted to keep it. It came as U.S. forces entered a second week of strikes on Iran. The aid and the war are one argument, split across two votes.
national.constitutional: The purse is Congress's oldest check. The founders gave the House first claim on spending so that the chamber closest to the voter would decide what the nation pays for — and, through it, what the nation fights for. The amendment failed, but the vote is the mechanism working as designed: the money for a foreign war argued in the open and recorded, name by name. What has thinned since 1941 is not the power but the use of it.
national.predictive: The 104 votes are a floor, not a ceiling. As the Iran war's cost climbs, expect the bloc willing to strip or condition foreign military aid to grow, and to keep crossing party lines. The next test is the full spending bill.

national.headline: Trump cuts Utah's two big monuments by nearly three million acres
national.fact: President Trump signed an executive order on July 13 shrinking two national monuments in southern Utah — Bears Ears and Grand Staircase-Escalante — by close to three million acres combined. The White House framed it as returning land to local control for grazing and recreation.
national.context: The monuments have grown and shrunk with each administration since President Clinton created Grand Staircase in 1996. Obama expanded, Trump cut, Biden restored, Trump cut again. The acreage is a proxy for an older question: who governs the federal land inside a state — Washington, or the people who live on it.
national.constitutional: The founders left most land questions to the states. The modern monument is a creature of a 1906 statute that lets one official set aside land by signature. What one signature makes, another unmakes — which is why the boundary has had no rest for thirty years. A line that moves with each election was never meant to be permanent; only Congress can make it so.
national.predictive: Expect the courts, not the order, to set the working line — and expect it to move again with the next president. Durable protection needs a statute. An executive order lasts exactly as long as the administration that signs it.

national.headline: EU bans Sudanese gold to starve a fourth-year war of its cash
national.fact: The European Union banned imports of Sudanese gold on July 13 and barred sales of mercury and cyanide to Sudan, moving to cut the revenue funding a civil war now in its fourth year. The United Nations counts more than 14 million people displaced.
national.context: Gold is how the war pays itself. The Sudanese army and the Rapid Support Forces both mine it and sell it, and Europe is a buyer. The ban also reaches the third countries that relabel Sudanese gold on its way into the EU.
national.predictive: Sanctions on a commodity as portable and fungible as gold tend to reroute trade more than stop it. Watch the Gulf refiners. If Sudanese gold keeps moving through them to other markets, the ban has shifted the map without shrinking the money.

economic.headline: Oil hits a one-month high as Hormuz shipping collapses
economic.fact: Brent crude reached about $85.92 a barrel on July 14, its highest in a month, as the fighting dimmed the outlook for the Strait of Hormuz, Al Jazeera reported. Shipping through the strait fell more than half — 57 transits over the weekend. The U.S. revoked its waiver on Iranian-oil transactions, effective after July 17.
economic.context: The strait is the fact under the fact. A fifth of the world's oil moves through a channel twenty-one miles wide at its narrowest. When it tightens, the price is paid everywhere — at the pump, in the grocery aisle, in the next rate decision — no matter who is doing the fighting.
economic.predictive: The waiver lapses July 17. If transits stay near zero past that date, Brent tests $90, and the Fed's July 29 hold gets harder to hold. This is the war's real reach: not the missiles, the price of a barrel.

economic.headline: Fed expected to hold rates July 29 — with a war attached to the decision
economic.fact: The Federal Reserve meets July 29. As of July 15, futures markets put the odds near 83 percent that it holds its rate range at 3.50 to 3.75 percent, where it has sat since June.
economic.context: The Fed is waiting, and the thing it waits on just moved. Inflation still runs above the 2 percent target, and a war in the Gulf now threatens the oil price that feeds it. A hold is the bet that the war's price shock stays contained.
economic.predictive: The strait sets this meeting as much as the data does. If Hormuz stays shut and oil runs through $90 before July 29, the easy hold gets an inflation problem attached — and the 83 percent you are reading now moves.

constitutional_feature.headline: The Court upheld birthright citizenship, 6–3. The dissent argued the ratifiers.
constitutional_feature.fact: On June 30 the Supreme Court ruled 6 to 3 in Trump v. Barbara that the Fourteenth Amendment grants citizenship to children born on U.S. soil to parents in the country illegally, striking down the executive order the president signed on his first day in office.
constitutional_feature.constitutional: The majority read the amendment's words — "subject to the jurisdiction thereof" — to reach nearly everyone born on American ground. The three dissenters read the same words against the debate that produced them. When the Senate wrote the clause in 1866, Jacob Howard, who introduced it, said it would not cover "foreigners, aliens, who belong to the families of ambassadors"; Lyman Trumbull defined the jurisdiction as owing "allegiance to nobody else." The men who ratified the amendment were answering the question of the freed slave, not the question of the illegal migrant, which did not yet exist in law. The Court has now given its answer. Whether it is the answer the ratifiers would have given is the argument the dissent keeps open — and a 6-to-3 vote does not close it.
constitutional_feature.predictive: A 6-3 ruling settles the case, not the question. Expect the dissent's reasoning to become the standard citation for a constitutional-amendment drive and for state-level tests built to hand the Court a later chance to revisit it. Birthright citizenship is now a political project on the right, not a settled legal assumption.
